text:
Summary  
The source text is a long-form policy/analysis document focused on catastrophic AI-risk stemming from organizational failures.  It surveys historical accidents, describes how weak safety culture and poor information-security can translate into AI disasters, and proposes layered (“Swiss-cheese”) sociotechnical safeguards.  It recommends concrete governance and engineering practices such as appointing a CRO, staged releases with external red-teaming, stronger publication controls, and allocating substantial resources to safety research.  These proposals are extracted below as a connected knowledge fabric linking headline risks → causes → theory → design concepts → mechanisms → evidence → actionable interventions.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[83]  
The data source is discursive and policy-oriented rather than empirical, so many links rely on medium evidence.  Nevertheless, all core reasoning chains have been captured without leaving isolated nodes or shortcuts from risks to interventions.  Node names were standardized for cross-corpus merge-ability.  

Inference strategy justification  
Where the paper offered recommendations implicitly (e.g. “labs should slow roll-outs”), moderate inference (edge confidence 2) converted them into explicit interventions.  Historical analogies were treated as validation evidence because the authors use them as support for the proposed safety measures.

Extraction completeness explanation  
34 nodes (≈1 every 170 words) cover all distinct claims that participate in causal-interventional reasoning.  Eight fully-spelled pathways converge into a single, interconnected fabric; every node is referenced by ≥1 edge and no intervention links directly back to a risk.

Key limitations  
• Some causal directions in organizational sociology are multifaceted; edges capture the dominant relation only.  
• Validation relies on historical precedent, not controlled AI experiments; confidence is therefore ≤3.  
• Interventions are policy-style, so lifecycle/maturity assignment required judgement.
